worksheet.title: Trace the Bug
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — read, predict, and fix code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can trace a loop step by step to find the bug.

parts.title: Walk through the code
text: To find a bug, TRACE the code: go through the loop one repeat at a time and keep track of what Bit has done.
Trace the loop below. After all the repeats, did Bit do what it should? If not, you have found the bug.

parts.title: Trace this — it SHOULD draw a square
parts.output: Trace: side 1, side 2, side 3 … then it stops.

parts.title: Trace it
parts.prompt: Go through the loop. After repeat 1: 1 side. After repeat 2: 2 sides. After repeat 3: ______ sides. A square needs 4 sides — what is the bug, and the fix?

parts.title: Trace the counts
parts.prompt: A loop is  repeat 4 { jump, jump }. Trace the jumps: after each repeat add 2. How many jumps in total? If Bit should only jump 4 times, what is the fix?

parts.title: Predict, then run
parts.prompt: Trace  for i in range(5): bit.forward(50); bit.right(90). How many sides does Bit draw? Is that right for a square? What is the fix?

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: Trace  for i in range(4): bit.forward(50); bit.right(60). It has 4 sides but the shape does not close. The range is right — so what is the bug?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Tracing means walking through the code one repeat at a time. If the end result is not the goal, the place where it goes wrong is the bug.

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students TRACE a loop one repeat at a time to find where it goes wrong (C3.2), then name the fix — covering wrong count, too many, overshoot, and wrong turn.

parts.title: Curriculum (Ontario Math 2020, Strand C3)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: Python Turtle / a block app projected; the printed worksheet + a pencil. A trace table on the board (repeat # → what happened) helps.

parts.title: Run it (about 30 min)
text: 1. Model a trace table: repeat 1 → side 1, repeat 2 → side 2, … for the range(3) square.
2. The trace ends at 3 sides — a square needs 4. Name bug + fix together.
3. Students do Exercises 1–4 (Ex 4 is the stretch), solo or in pairs.
4. Share answers; land the big idea: trace to the end, then compare to the goal.

parts.title: Answer key (checked by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — 3 sides; the bug is range(3); fix to range(4).
Ex 3 — 5 sides (one too many / overshoot); fix to range(4).
Ex 4 (challenge) — the TURN is wrong (right 60); a square needs right 90.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: guessing instead of tracing each repeat.
Support: fill the trace table together for the first repeat, then students continue.
Extend: trace range(6) f50 r60 — a hexagon — and confirm it closes.

parts.title: Success looks like
parts.text: The student traces a loop to the end, compares the result to the goal, and names both the bug and the fix (Ex 1–4).
